explanations.answer: He has been calling for help a while
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. "How long" is what you say when you've already been waiting. Habakkuk, the prophet, says he calls for help "…but You do not hear…" I've said "how long" to a slow oven, but his wait weighs a whole lot more than mine.

explanations.answer: He is praying for the very first time
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. "How long" points to a wait that has already been going on. Habakkuk says he has been calling for help and crying out. The words themselves suggest it's been a while.

explanations.answer: He wants to know how long the vision lasts
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, but look at the whole sentence. The vision is how Habakkuk receives this message. His question is “How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear…” That's about his cry for help, not about the length of a vision.

Yes, friend. Habakkuk says he cries out to the LORD, “Violence!” and he says the LORD does not save. Those are his words about what he's living through. I think this is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't hurry past it.

Look again, friend. This one is true, because Habakkuk really does say it. He asks how long he must cry out to the LORD, “Violence!” “but You do not save?” Those are his own words, and they're honest and heavy.
That's it, baker. Habakkuk asks, “Why do You tolerate wrongdoing?” That's the second question in a row, and he doesn't water it down. He's telling the LORD plainly what he sees.

Close to the mood, friend, but that's not the word in the verse. Habakkuk asks, “Why do You tolerate wrongdoing?” The word is wrongdoing. He's pointing at what's happening around him, and the verse doesn't use the word doubt.

I can see why you'd pick it, since the whole verse is heavy. But the verse says, “Why do You tolerate wrongdoing?” Sorrow isn't in it. Habakkuk is looking at destruction and violence, and he names wrongdoing.

explanations.answer: The wicked hem in the righteous
explanations.explanation: You've got it, friend. Habakkuk says, “For the wicked hem in the righteous, so that justice is perverted.” That's the reason he gives for why justice comes out twisted. Notice he doesn't blame bad luck. He points straight at the wicked.

Not this time, friend. Habakkuk never says the prophets went quiet. He gives one reason: “For the wicked hem in the righteous, so that justice is perverted.” And he's a prophet himself, speaking up right here.

explanations.answer: The king has left the city
explanations.explanation: Fair try, baker, but no king leaves anywhere in these verses. The passage gives no city and no king at this point. Habakkuk's reason is that “…the wicked hem in the righteous…”

explanations.answer: You would never believe it even if told
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The LORD says He is doing a work “…that you would never believe even if someone told you.” That's not me hyping it up. Those are His words, and they're about to land.

explanations.answer: Only the wise will understand it at first
explanations.explanation: I like the thinking, baker, but the LORD doesn't say that. He says nothing about a wise group who gets it first. The verse says “…you would never believe even if someone told you.” Being told doesn't help, wise or not.

explanations.answer: Everyone will see it coming from far away
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite, friend. The LORD calls it a work you "…would never believe even if someone told you." If everyone saw it coming, it wouldn't be astounding. He even says, “…be utterly astounded!”

Right on, friend. The LORD says, “For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans…” They're the nation He names as the unbelievable work. Keep that name close, because we're about to learn a lot about them.
Good try, friend, but the Philistines, another nation, never show up in these verses. The LORD says, “…I am raising up the Chaldeans…” That's the name to remember.
Not this one, baker. The Moabites, another nation, aren't named anywhere in this passage. The LORD says, “…I am raising up the Chaldeans…” That's the nation He points to.

explanations.answer: To take homes that belong to others
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD says they march “…to seize dwellings not their own.” They march across the earth to take places that belong to others. It's a hard picture.

explanations.answer: To take back land they once owned
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The text says nothing about land they once owned. It says they march “…to seize dwellings not their own.” That's the reason the LORD gives.

explanations.answer: To hunt down one rival king
explanations.explanation: I see where that came from, since kings do come up later in the passage. But the reason given here is “…to seize dwellings not their own.” It isn't about one rival. They march through the breadth of the earth.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, “from themselves they derive justice and sovereignty.” Their idea of justice comes from the Chaldeans themselves. That's the Chaldeans, the ruthless nation the LORD says He is raising up (Habakkuk 1:6). They don't look to anyone else to tell them what's fair.
This one's true, friend, so let's look at the verse. The LORD says, “from themselves they derive justice and sovereignty.” Their justice comes from themselves, just as the statement says.

You've got it, baker. “Their horses are swifter than leopards, fiercer than wolves of the night.” Swifter means fast and fiercer means fierce. I'm a stamper on a gold base, so I'm not winning any race against a leopard.
That's backwards on the slow part, friend. The verse says the horses are “…swifter than leopards…” Swifter means faster, so slow doesn't fit.
Fierce, yes, but not fearful. The verse says they're “…fiercer than wolves of the night.” Nothing in it shows these horses scared of anything.
That's it, friend. “They fly like a vulture, swooping down to devour.” The picture is a vulture swooping down on its prey. The LORD is showing how they come at their target.
Fair guess, since vultures do circle. But this verse describes the dive. It says “…swooping down to devour.” Nobody's keeping watch in this picture.
That's a peaceful picture, baker, and this verse isn't peaceful. The vulture is “…swooping down to devour.” It's heading toward its prey, not toward a nest.
Right, friend. The LORD says “they gather prisoners like sand.” Think of trying to count the crumbs after a big batch, and then picture sand instead. That's how many captives it is.
Other way around, friend. Sand comes in huge amounts, and the LORD says “they gather prisoners like sand.” You can't call a small number sand.
Interesting, baker, but the verse doesn't say who the captives are. It only says “they gather prisoners like sand.” The sand picture is about how many, not about rank.
Not quite, friend. A strong fortress doesn't turn them back. The LORD says, “They laugh at every fortress and build up siege ramps to seize it.” They're not stopping at the wall.

That's right, baker. The statement is false because the Chaldeans “…laugh at every fortress and build up siege ramps to seize it.” A strong fortress doesn't make them turn back. They build siege ramps to seize it.

You've got it, friend. The LORD says, “They are guilty; their own strength is their god.” Their power is what they bow to. And I'd say a god you can only count on while you're winning isn't much of one.
Not this one, baker. The verse says they scoff at kings and make rulers an object of scorn. Those rulers aren't what the LORD names as their god. The verse says, “their own strength is their god.”
I get the thinking, friend, but the verse says they laugh at every fortress. They're not worshiping what they're seizing. The LORD says, “their own strength is their god.”
